kept.title: KeyFromID accepts non-canonical PeerIDs: one member key gives unboundedly many admitted identities
kept.question: spec-to-code
kept.rule: §3.1 (spec.md:210-212): « Un PeerID DOIT être canonique (le ré-encodage de la clé extraite redonne la même chaîne) ». keys.go:59-60 also claims that « two spellings of one identity cannot become two map keys ».
kept.evidence: internal/transport/p2p/keys.go:61-69 parseID only checks `p.String() != string(id)`, which re-encodes the multihash bytes, not the key; keys.go:42-56 then calls ExtractPublicKey and ValidatePublicKey and never compares IDFromKey(raw) with id. go-libp2p core/peer/peer.go:87-99 ExtractPublicKey goes to core/crypto/key.go:123-131 `proto.Unmarshal(data, pmes)`, which accepts fields in any order and unknown fields. The references are stricter: protocol/conformance/reference.go:463-469 requires exactly `00 24 08 01 12 20` and 38 bytes, and frontend/packages/protocol/reference.ts:476-489 requires the same prefix. Reachable path: mdns.go:61-63 HandlePeerFound → addrbook.go:726-727 rememberLAN → addrbook.go:465-482 noteLAN, gated only by member() (addrbook.go:643-646) → Admission.Admit (internal/app/wiring.go:54-57) → KeyFromID. On reload, decodeBookPeer (addrbook.go:151) accepts the same spellings.
kept.scenario: An unattested device on the LAN sends mDNS announcements whose /p2p/ component is the multihash `00 24 || 12 20 <memberKey> 08 01` (protobuf fields reversed), or `00 26 || 08 01 12 20 <key> 18 NN` (an unknown field), and so on. Each spelling is a different peer.ID under 64 characters that passes ValidPeerID, parseID and KeyFromID, and Admit reports it as the member. Each one becomes its own address-book entry (bookMaxPeers = 64, addrbook.go:36) and is written to addresses.json. evictLocked (addrbook.go:488-496) then evicts the real members' mDNS-only entries first, so the per-identity bound the RC1 fix relies on no longer holds. The Go application decoder also disagrees with both conformance references, which refuse these inputs.
kept.fix: In KeyFromID, after extracting raw, require IDFromKey(raw) == id (the §3.1 re-encoding rule). Better: move a pure PeerID codec into the protocol module (base58 identity multihash, exact 38-byte `00 24 08 01 12 20` form) and use it from both p2p and the conformance runner. Add reject vectors `peer-id-noncanonical-protobuf` (reversed fields, unknown field) and `peer-id-cid` (CID form) to crypto.json, and run them through the application decoder.

verdicts.reason: The defect is real. internal/transport/p2p/keys.go:61-69 parseID only round-trips the multihash bytes (`p.String() != string(id)`), and keys.go:42-56 never compares IDFromKey(raw) with id. In the pinned fork, core/peer/peer.go:87-99 calls crypto.UnmarshalPublicKey, which does `proto.Unmarshal` (core/crypto/key.go:123-131, google.golang.org/protobuf v1.36.11). That accepts reordered fields and unknown fields, so a non-canonical protobuf envelope around a member key passes. This breaks §3.1 and the promise in keys.go:59-60, and disagrees with conformance/reference.go:463-469, which requires the exact 00 24 08 01 12 20 prefix and 38 bytes. It is reachable without attestation: mdns.go:61-63 → rememberLAN (addrbook.go:726-727) → noteLAN (465-482), whose member() check (643-646) goes through Admission.Admit → KeyFromID (wiring.go:54-57). The impact is overstated, so severity drops to minor. LAN entries are memory only (addrbook.go:76-87, and save skips entries without authenticated addrs at :284), so nothing is written to addresses.json. Dials to a forged spelling fail at the libp2p handshake, which derives the canonical ID. evictLocked (488-496) evicts mDNS-only entries before authenticated ones. The same LAN attacker can already overwrite a real member's mDNS addresses by announcing its canonical ID (merge with fresh first, bookMaxLAN=2, :476). What remains is a spec and decoder divergence with marginal extra DoS.

The defect is real. internal/transport/p2p/keys.go:61-69 parseID only checks that peer.Decode(id).String() == id, which re-encodes the same multihash bytes back to base58, so the protobuf inside is never re-encoded. keys.go:42-56 never compares IDFromKey(raw) with id. In the forked go-libp2p that is actually used (oioio-space/go-libp2p@v0.51.1-…), core/peer/peer.go ExtractPublicKey calls core/crypto/key.go:123-131 UnmarshalPublicKey, which is proto.Unmarshal of a proto2 message. Proto2 accepts reordered fields, unknown fields and repeated fields. That breaks the MUST of spec.md:210-212 and the comment at keys.go:59-60. The conformance runner is stricter: reference.go:462-470 requires `00 24 08 01 12 20` and 38 bytes. Path checked: mdns.go HandlePeerFound → rememberLAN (addrbook.go:726-727) → noteLAN (addrbook.go:465-482). noteLAN is gated only by member() (addrbook.go:643-646), which calls Admission.Admit (wiring.go:54-57) → KeyFromID, so it accepts the member key. Each spelling is its own map key. evictLocked (addrbook.go:488-496) evicts entries that only mDNS gave first, so real members found only by mDNS can be pushed out. Nothing else prevents this: the gater and the handshake derive the canonical ID, which stops connections under a fake spelling but not book pollution. Two corrections: mDNS-only entries are not persisted (addrbook.go:463 says « not stored », and addrbook.go:550 skips them), so the claim about addresses.json and reload is overstated, and the impact is limited to evicting LAN-only entries. It stays major: it violates an explicit MUST at an identity entry point, the app decoder disagrees with both references, and an unattested peer breaks a per-identity bound.

kept.title: Lobby Ask runs a 64 MiB Argon2id per stranger key before any cap: host memory and CPU exhaustion
kept.question: hostile-peer
kept.rule: Threat model in the brief: unattested peers are strictly bounded. §17 « Épuisement » (spec.md:2147): every queue, map and byte has a bound and an owner. §12 order: nothing costly before the check that can refuse.
kept.evidence: internal/invite/flow.go:388-399: `fp := identity.Fingerprint(key, h.cfg.Lang)` runs at line 389, before `if len(h.asks) >= maxAsks` (392) and before the per-peer dedup (395-398). internal/identity/fingerprint.go:25 sets `fpMemoryKiB = 64 * 1024`; the comment at fingerprint.go:92-94 says « distinct keys compute in parallel », and line 145 calls `compute(key[:])` outside the lock with no concurrency bound. Each new key is a cache miss (fingerprint.go:127-145). Ask is served while Visible (flow.go:303-307), and the stranger window admits any authenticated peer (p2p/node.go:530-538, 548-553). Limits: ConnsInbound = maxPeers = 64 (node.go:91, 489); 2 lobby streams per peer (lobby.go:30).
kept.scenario: While « visible to join » is open (10 min, renewable; Session.SetVisible is an exported binding, internal/app/session.go:107), an attacker opens up to 64 inbound connections, each with a freshly generated key, and sends one Ask on each. Every Ask allocates 64 MiB and runs Argon2id before being turned away as Busy. That is about 4 GiB live at once, plus all cores busy, and it repeats with new keys for the whole window. Today the frontend never calls SetVisible or Session.Requests (grep found no use), so the path is latent; it becomes reachable once the join UI ships. When it does, it meets the brief's « critical » (host exhaustion by an unattested peer).
kept.fix: Reserve the ask slot (cap check, then per-peer dedup) under the lock before any fingerprint work, and compute the fingerprint lazily when a person views the request. Put a process-wide semaphore (for example 2) around Argon2 in fingerprints.get. Test: N concurrent Asks with distinct keys perform at most maxAsks plus the semaphore's computations (count calls through NewTestFingerprints).

verdicts.reason: The code does what is claimed. flow.go:388-389 addAsk calls identity.Fingerprint(key, …) before `len(h.asks) >= maxAsks` (392, maxAsks=8 at :29) and before the per-peer dedup (395-398). fingerprint.go:127-145 computes a 64 MiB Argon2id (fpMemoryKiB at :25) outside the lock for every cache miss, with no concurrency bound. ask() (flow.go:353-366) checks only KeyOf/ValidatePublicKey and existing membership before calling it, and p2p/lobby.go has no global bound on lobby handlers. It is not reachable in the shipped app, which lowers severity to minor. KindAsk is served only while h.Visible() (flow.go:303-307). Visible is set only by Host.SetVisible (flow.go:197), called only from Session.SetVisible (session.go:152-156), and nothing in frontend/src calls it (only the generated binding exists). It is a latent ordering defect that becomes host exhaustion the day the « visible to join » UI ships. The fix is to move the fingerprint after the cap and dedup checks.

The code ordering is as described. internal/invite/flow.go:388-389 calls identity.Fingerprint(key, …) before the maxAsks check (flow.go:392, maxAsks = 8 at flow.go:29) and before the per-peer dedup (395-398). fingerprint.go:25 sets 64 MiB, and fingerprint.go:127-145 computes each cache miss outside the lock with no concurrency bound: singleflight works only per key. Ask is served only while Visible (flow.go:303-307). ask() (flow.go:~355) validates only the key and membership before addAsk. lobby.go:30-31 bounds streams per peer, not overall, and the system allows 64 inbound connections (node.go:~489), so about 64 fresh keys means about 4 GiB of Argon2 at once. Reachability is latent: SetVisible is at session.go:152, not :107, and grep finds no frontend caller. The auditor acknowledges this. It is not a known finding (the admission-invite review covers only admit/MaxReply). It is kept as major rather than critical because it cannot be reached until the join UI ships.

kept.title: No vector or test pins the R rules of §3.3 for a valid key (cofactorless equation, byte comparison, R not validated)
kept.question: proof
kept.rule: §3.3 (spec.md:249-256): accepted iff (a) A valid, (b) S < L, (c) the encoding of [S]B − [k]A equals R byte for byte (cofactorless); « R n'est pas validé autrement » ; « un désaccord sur une signature est un désaccord sur la liste » ; the twelve speccheck cases « DOIT les reproduire ».
kept.evidence: crypto.json: every speccheck-0…11 vector is reject, and each is refused through the key (reasons « small order », « mixed order », « non-canonical encoding ») or through S (speccheck-6/7 « crypto/ed25519.Verify = false »). The only accept vector is sig-domain-1, an honest signature. protocol/sig/verify_test.go:47-104 adds only length and wrong-message cases. protocol/sig/verify.go:51-53 is the byte comparison, and nothing exercises it with torsion on R. reference.ts:59-65 records the intent (« noble verify() checks the cofactored equation »), but no vector separates the two.
kept.scenario: A Byzantine writer signs an op with its own valid key a: it picks r and a torsion point T, sets R = rB + T, k = H(R‖A‖M) and S = r + k·a. A cofactored verifier ([8](SB − kA − R) = O, as in noble's verify, ZIP-215 libraries or ed25519-dalek's non-strict verify) accepts, while protocol/sig rejects. Likewise R = encoding of the neutral point with S = k·a is accepted by the spec and refused by libraries that reject small-order R (dalek verify_strict). A third-party or future TypeScript implementation built on such a library passes every vector, then diverges from inkwell on the member list. The mutant « replace the byte comparison at verify.go:53 by a cofactored point check » would survive every vector and test.
kept.fix: Generate, with RFC 8032 seed A, signature+key vectors that have a valid key and test R: (i) R carries a torsion component and passes only the cofactored equation → reject; (ii) R = neutral (01 00…00), S = k·a → accept; (iii) R = a non-canonical encoding of the neutral point (sign bit set, or y = p+1) with a matching S → reject. Add a cross-domain reject vector (sig-domain-1's signature under domain attest). Name the tests after the §3.3 sentences they prove.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. In crypto.json every speccheck-0…11 vector is reject, and each is decided by the key (reasons small order, mixed order, non-canonical) or by S (speccheck-6/7). No vector pairs a valid prime-order A with a torsion-bearing or small-order R. sig-domain-1 is the only signature accept. protocol/sig/verify_test.go:47-104 adds only length and wrong-message cases. A grep for torsion/cofactor in tests finds torsion only on keys (internal/identity/public_test.go:55-64, 135-152). A cofactored mutant of verify.go:53 would survive every vector. Severity drops to minor: inkwell's own Go (verify.go:30-58) and TS reference (reference.ts:66-77) both implement the cofactorless byte comparison, and no frontend app code verifies signatures with noble's verify(). The gap only lets a future or third-party implementation pass the corpus while diverging.

The vector gap is confirmed. In crypto.json every speccheck-0…11 case is reject. Cases 0-5 and 8-11 are refused on the key (small order, mixed order, non-canonical). Cases 6-7 use the prime-order key 442a… and are refused on S (reason « crypto/ed25519.Verify = false », non-canonical S). The only accept vector is sig-domain-1, an honest signature. A grep for torsion and cofactor finds only key-side tests (internal/identity/public_test.go:55-64, 135-152), nothing that puts torsion on R under a valid key. protocol/sig/verify.go:51-53 is correct, but nothing exercises it with a torsioned or neutral R. Because §3.2 rejects mixed-order A, speccheck cases 4/5 no longer separate cofactored from cofactorless verification. A cofactored verifier, such as noble verify(), which reference.ts:59-65 notes, would pass the whole corpus. spec.md:250-256 states that a signature disagreement is a member-list disagreement, so the gap matters for any third-party implementation.

kept.title: The ticket codec does not validate the host key at decode (§3.2 entry point « hôte d'un ticket »)
kept.question: spec-to-code
kept.rule: §3.2 (spec.md:229-236): every key entering the protocol DOIT be validated « au plus tôt, à chaque point d'entrée : … hôte d'un ticket », and an invalid key is refused as malformed input. §3.1: a PeerID DOIT be canonical with a valid key. ADR 0034 step 2 (docs/adr/0034-protocole-unifie.md:221) lists « ticket » among the N-1 callers.
kept.evidence: protocol/invite/ticket.go:153 `t.Host = transport.PeerID(r.take(int(r.u8())))` and :168 check only `transport.ValidPeerID(t.Host)` (printable ASCII, 1–64 bytes, protocol/peer.go:16-25) and the absence of '/'. The host key is first validated in the application, after the network exchange: internal/invite/flow.go:533-539 Joiner.verify (KeyOf, then ValidatePublicKey). lobby.json has a single ticket_text vector, ticket-text, and it is accept.
kept.scenario: ParseText accepts an invitation whose Host is `12D3KooW9tGaPdJo5jmCpadQ971nfiq4kLcQjeBPYTfutBTtckPH` (the neutral key), a CID spelling, or text such as « nobody ». In inkwell the gater (gate.go:37) or peer.Decode then refuses the connection, so the person sees a connection failure instead of « invitation invalide ». Any other user of the public protocol/invite module gets no §3.2 protection at all.
kept.fix: In decodeTicket, decode Host with the pure PeerID codec of the protocol module (canonical form, ValidatePublicKey on the extracted key) and refuse with ErrMalformed. Add lobby.json reject vectors: ticket-host-small-order, ticket-host-noncanonical, ticket-host-not-peerid.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed against the spec text. §3.2 (spec.md:229-233) lists « hôte d'un ticket » among the points where a key MUST be validated at the earliest point, and ADR 0034 step 2 (:221) lists the ticket among the N-1 callers. protocol/invite/ticket.go:153 and :168 check only ValidPeerID and the absence of '/'. The first key check comes after the network exchange, in Joiner.verify (internal/invite/flow.go:533-539), and app/invites.go:287-317 adds no earlier check. Severity drops to minor: the security outcome is preserved because the connection gater and KeyFromID refuse a small-order or non-Ed25519 host before any connection. The effect is a wrong error class (connection failure instead of malformed invitation) and missing protection for reusers of the public protocol/invite module.

The divergence is real. protocol/invite/ticket.go:153 and :168 check only ValidPeerID (protocol/peer.go:16-25) and the absence of '/'. Both spec.md:229-236 (« hôte d'un ticket ») and §8.3 (spec.md ~1118: `host str8 (PeerID, clé valide §3.2)`) require the key to be valid at decode. The app parses with invite.ParseText (internal/app/invites.go:291) and validates the host key only after the network exchange (flow.go:533-539). The severity is lowered to minor. There is no security effect: the host connection still goes through the gater and the handshake, and only an invalid ticket is affected, so the cost is a wrong error message and missing protection for third-party users of protocol/invite. lobby.json has a single accept ticket vector.

kept.title: Vector schema and expectations of the §3 corpus are not reproduced, and the application decoders are not run against them
kept.question: proof
kept.rule: §21 (spec.md:2267-2273): each vector carries `decoder` (no « ? » in the schema), `expect` is « ce qu'une implémentation DOIT reproduire », and decoders are named (spec.md:2320, where no empty decoder appears). §16: bounds are exported constants of protocol, one test per row.
kept.evidence: protocol/vectors/crypto.json:18-30: sig-domain-1 has no `decoder` field; the Go runner maps it to the key "" (reference.go:46) and so does the TS runner (`case undefined`, reference.ts:493). peer-id-A (crypto.json:57-66) carries input_hex and expect.public_hex, but reference.go:462-470 decodes only expect.peer_id and never compares it with input_hex or public_hex; reference.ts:476-489 is the same. The only Go tests that read crypto.json are protocol/sig/verify_test.go and internal/identity/public_test.go; KeyFromID and Device.Sign never see the corpus (p2p's small_order_test.go hardcodes one ID). protocol/limits.go:221-222 exports MaxPeerIDBytes = 64, but ValidPeerID uses a private copy maxPeerIDLen (protocol/peer.go:7,17).
kept.scenario: A peer_id decoder that extracts the wrong 32 bytes, as long as they are a valid key, passes peer-id-A. A third-party runner that follows §21 strictly fails on sig-domain-1 because it has no decoder. Changing MaxPeerIDBytes does not change the enforced bound.
kept.fix: Give sig-domain-1 a named decoder (for example `signature+domain`) and add it to the §21 list. Make the peer_id check compare the decoded multihash with input_hex and the key with public_hex, in Go and TS. Run the crypto.json peer_id and signature vectors through p2p.KeyFromID and identity.Device.Sign (sign with seed A, compare signature_hex). Make ValidPeerID use MaxPeerIDBytes.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. sig-domain-1 has no decoder field, and both runners special-case it: reference.go:46 maps it to the key "" and reference.ts handles it as `case undefined`. That contradicts §21's schema (spec.md:2267-2269), where decoder is not optional. The peer_id checks (reference.go:462-470 and reference.ts:476-489) validate only the envelope and the key of expect.peer_id, and never compare the extracted key with expect.public_hex. The only Go tests that read crypto.json are protocol/sig/verify_test.go, internal/identity/public_test.go and conformance/reference_mutation_test.go. No test feeds the corpus to p2p.KeyFromID. protocol/peer.go:7,17 enforces a private maxPeerIDLen that no test ties to the exported MaxPeerIDBytes (limits.go:221-222). This is a proof gap with no runtime effect today, so minor is right.

Confirmed as minor gaps in proof and schema. crypto.json:18-30 sig-domain-1 has no `decoder` field, while §21 (spec.md:2267-2269) lists `decoder` as required. Both runners treat its absence as "" or undefined (reference.go:46, reference.ts:493). reference.go:462-470 peer() never compares expect.public_hex or input_hex with the decoded key; it only validates the extracted bytes, so a decoder that returns the wrong valid 32 bytes would pass. protocol/peer.go:7,17 uses a private maxPeerIDLen = 64 rather than the exported MaxPeerIDBytes (limits.go:221-222). The part saying KeyFromID is never run against the corpus overlaps finding 0's root cause; the other points are distinct.

dropped.title: Domain separation is built outside protocol, without the §20.4 domain check, and the version suffix is ambiguous

verdicts.reason: No reachable defect. Every Sign or signingMessage caller passes a constant registry domain (e.g. protocol/cmd/vectors/main.go:187, 621, 680, 716, 750; trust/op.go:382-384), and §20.4 (spec.md:2232) is a rule on the registry, which those constants satisfy. No peer or person supplies a domain. The prefix being built in identity/device.go:176-183 and trust/op.go as well as in protocol/sig is duplication for a /simplify review, not a protocol violation. The version ambiguity is not real: §3.3 (spec.md:246) is normative that every signature uses the /v1 suffix. §1.4.4 (spec.md:92-98) separates object versions by the version byte inside the signed bytes, so op v2 being « identique à la version 1 » (spec.md:303-306) leaves no guess. The auditor itself states there is no reachable effect.

Refuted: no defect is reachable, as the finding itself concedes. Every Sign call passes a constant domain from the §20.4 registry (protocol/cmd/vectors/main.go:187,621,680,716,750; device.go:174-183 documents the constraint), so no domain contains '/' or NUL. A collision would need a non-constant domain, and none exists. The version-suffix ambiguity is also weak. §1.4.4 (spec.md:92-98) puts the version byte inside the signed bytes after ProjectID for trust-op, so v2 is already separated by its version byte, and §1.4.4 changes the suffix only when the signature covers something other than the object bytes. §4.2's « identique à la version 1 » is consistent with keeping trust-op/v1. Duplicating the prefix helper (device.go:177, op.go:382-384) is a code-organisation matter with no conformance effect.

dropped.title: The four-word fingerprint is unspecified, and no device shows it, so the human check of Ask does not exist

verdicts.reason: Not a reachable protocol defect. The four-word fingerprint (internal/identity/fingerprint.go) is a local display derivation and never crosses the wire, so no byte from a peer depends on it, and §3.4 rightly lists only wire digests. The « human check of Ask does not exist » half has the same latent precondition as finding [1]: Ask is served only while Visible (flow.go:303-307), and nothing in frontend/src calls SetVisible or Requests, so the whole Ask flow is unshipped. This is a UI-completeness gap of an unshipped feature, not a P1 spec-to-code divergence. Whether the word derivation should be specified for interoperation between implementations is a design question for when the join UI is built. With that uncertainty, refuted.

The spec gap is real. Grep of spec.md finds no Argon2, BIP39 or four-word fingerprint; §8.2 (spec.md:1107) says only « Ask attend l'accord d'une personne ». The glossary (docs/glossary.md:23) defines empreinte as 4 words derived from the key, and fingerprint.go:20-28 and 160-169 fixes a derivation that another implementation would have to guess (README point 10), with no vector. The claim that the human check does not exist is overstated: the whole Ask and Requests UI is unshipped (grep finds no frontend caller of SetVisible or Requests), so no Ask can be answered today, by name or otherwise. It stays minor as a specification and design gap that will matter when the join UI ships.

parts.name: Signed objects and the member-list fold
parts.coverage:
Read in full: docs/plans/2026-11-14-protocol-audit-brief.md; docs/protocol/README.md; spec.md §4.1–§4.10 (lines 269–519), §3.3–§3.4, §16.1–§16.3, §19–§21; protocol/trust/{op.go,list.go,fold.go,attest.go,sync.go,doc.go}; internal/trust/protocol.go (forwarding only, no private codec); internal/app/{wiring.go,attest.go,suspend.go}; protocol/limits.go lines 140–240; protocol/sig/{public.go,verify.go}; protocol/conformance/reference.go (op, sync, attestation and fold cases); frontend/packages/protocol/{reference.ts,src/conformance.ts,conformance.test.ts,README.md}; the vector lists of trust.json, fold.json, attest.json and policy.json (ids, status, decoder, verdict); the headers of alloy/README.md, Decisions.als and tla/RepoGen.tla; ADR 0034's migration table; the mux package doc. To avoid repeating known findings I checked TR1 (codex-coverage.md and autonomous-decisions.md row 34: circular witness, divergent saturation, revocation not durable, non-atomic suspension, equal-seq attestation equivocation), the admission/invite ultrareview and gates/W58/REVIEW.md. kept.title: A reader can starve every peer's document sync: costly key validation runs before dedup, with no per-peer budget or sanction, and control frames always go before repo frames
kept.question: hostile-peer
kept.rule: Threat model: readers and unattested peers are strictly bounded. README rule 1, « Rien de partagé n'attend un pair ». §10.4 fairness. README rule 5: verification order size → form → signature, and nothing that fails reaches the next step. An op or attestation that is already known should cost nothing.
kept.evidence: protocol/trust/op.go:347-378 (Decode) calls validate, and op.go:197-201 validates both keys (sig.ValidatePublicKey, i.e. one ScalarMult each, protocol/sig/public.go:20-35). protocol/trust/list.go:137-142: apply validates again (two more key validations) before the `known(h)` dedup. sync.go:105-106 with 111-123: an ErrBadSignature from an op is not ErrMalformed, so the peer is never dropped. internal/app/attest.go:242-250: DecodeAttestation (one key validation), then Verify (two more plus the equation, protocol/trust/attest.go:138-141), and only then the dedup at att.add (attest.go:260); errors are only logged. internal/app/wiring.go:385-412: step() handles a queued trust or attest event before it ever polls the repo channel. internal/transport/mux/mux.go:16: « a full queue stops the reader, and with it every other channel ».
kept.scenario: Any active member, a reader included, replays a valid attestation (about 142 bytes), or sends well-formed attestations or ops with random signatures, in a tight loop. Each frame costs the victim's single Wiring goroutine three to four scalar multiplications (not measured; roughly 10^-4 s), and no frame ever leads to a drop or a budget. As long as the attest queue is never empty, step() never reaches the repo channel, so no peer's document frames reach the webview. When the 256-event attest queue fills, the mux reader stops every channel of every peer. The required rate is below 1 MB/s (an estimate).
kept.fix: Dedup by hash before any key validation (Hash needs no validation). Give attestations and trust Ops a per-peer budget per tick, and an exact-duplicate filter. Sanction repeated ErrBadSignature as a fault. Serve control and repo in bounded alternation (per-peer boxes, as ADR 0034 step 5 plans). Add a test where one reader floods duplicates and another peer's repo frames still pass within a bound.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. wiring.go:384-410: step() calls control() first and returns without polling repoCh whenever a trust or attest event is queued. attest.go:242-250: a decode error drops the peer, but a Verify failure (bad signature, ErrNotWriter) or a duplicate is only logged, and dedup (att.add, :260) comes after Verify. Each attestation costs a full ScalarMult key validation in decode, again in Verify (attest.go:49, :138) and once more in sig.Verify (sig/public.go:20-35). Ops get the same treatment: list.go:137-142 validates before the known(h) check, and sync.go:105-123 drops only on ErrMalformed. mux.go:16 says a full queue stops every channel. Readers are linked and full (wiring.go:510-517, restricted only when suspended), so they reach this path. Lowered to major: it is a liveness DoS by an admitted member, it ends when that member is removed, and the rates are estimates, not measurements.

Confirmed in the code. wiring.go:385-412: step() calls control() first and returns as soon as a trust or attest event is handled, so the repo channel is polled only when both control queues are empty. A reader is active (activate/refresh, wiring.go:515-557, opens attest unless suspended). A valid replayed attestation runs DecodeAttestation→validate (one ValidatePublicKey, with the ScalarMult at sig/public.go:20-35), then Verify→validate again plus sig.Verify (protocol/trust/attest.go:134-141), before the att.add dedup (internal/app/attest.go:260). The only consequence is a Debug log (attest.go:247-250), with no drop or budget. Trust ops likewise run validate (two key checks) before known(h) (list.go:137-142). Only ErrMalformed drops the peer (wiring.go:428-431, sync.go:105-123). The final mux-wide stall is known (inventaire N-4, N-5; ADR 0034 steps 4-5), but nothing recorded covers the CPU amplification of valid replays, made before any dedup and never sanctioned, or the control-over-repo priority that starves repo frames before any queue fills. Lowered to major: the rate is an unmeasured estimate, the harm is liveness only, and an admin can remove the reader.

kept.title: A reader's sync message makes the webview run Automerge decodeChange/load on unbounded RLE/deflate content before any bounded parse
kept.question: hostile-peer
kept.rule: §9.7 G1: change ≤ 16 MiB decompressed and ≤ 65 536 operations, « analyse bornée avant Automerge »; §16.2 garde row (spec.md:2117) « refus (avant Automerge) », Worker 256 MiB; threat model: readers strictly bounded
kept.evidence: frontend/src/net/WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:533-537 `#enforce` sends every sync/request from any member (comment :529-531 « readers may send them ») to `this.#coverage.filter`; coverage.ts:293 `msg.changes.flatMap(splitChunks).map(describeChunk)` decodes every chunk before coverage is known at :300; coverage.ts:396-404 `A.load<unknown>(bytes)` for a document chunk and `A.decodeChange(bytes)` for a change chunk. ADR 0028:125-128: « decodeChange matérialise les opérations ... une modification forgée de très nombreuses opérations (compressée en RLE en quelques octets) coûte sa mémoire avant d'être comptée ... la confiance accordée aux écrivants signés est le garde-fou ». No G1 pre-parser exists in frontend/src (grep for guard/G12 found none in net/).

The message carries one change chunk whose RLE action/insert columns declare millions of insert ops in a few kilobytes, or a deflated document chunk. describeChunk decodes it on the main thread before the coverage check, so the webview allocates the ops (or the inflated columns) until it freezes or runs out of memory. ADR 0028 accepts this risk only because « only a signed writer can send ». The code runs the decode for readers too, so that premise does not hold.

Inflate with a 16 MiB cap and refuse more than 65 536 ops. Decide coverage from this header data, call A.decodeChange only on covered changes, and call A.load only inside the bounded Worker. Add a test that a reader's 10^7-op RLE change is refused without allocating it, plus a mutant that removes the cap.

kept.scenario: A writer device signs attestations for one admitted document with increasing seq, each carrying 64 fresh random 32-byte heads that will never arrive. Go accepts each one (it brings a new head) and forwards it as an Attested envelope. The webview's `kept` stays at 256 entries, but `#covered` and `#open` gain 64 strings per attestation without end, so memory grows until the webview dies; the writer can repeat this for 1024 documents. The evicted heads also go on counting as covered, against §6.2 « usage ».
kept.fix: When `kept` evicts heads, recompute #covered/#open the way `revoke` does, or keep the phantom (#open) heads per signer, capped at 256. Track seq so eviction follows the « smallest seq » rule. Specify and implement a per-signer rate for forwarding newly kept attestations (§6.2/§10.6). Add a test: 10 000 attestations of fresh heads leave the coverage size bounded. Add a mutant that drops the recompute.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. coverage.ts:59-68 attest pushes each head, calls #cover(h), and trims only `kept` to 256. #cover (:128-137) adds to #covered and to #open, which only revoke (:76-81) clears. Go's attestStore.add (attest.go:42-51) accepts any higher Seq, and offerAttest (:256-272) notifies the webview with no rate limit. Growth is unbounded and evicted heads keep covering. Lowered to major: a writer-driven memory DoS that builds up over time, with no integrity breach.

Confirmed. coverage.ts:59-68 trims only `kept` to 256. `#cover` (:128-137) adds every attested head to `#covered` (and to `#open` when its deps are unknown). Only revoke (:76-81) clears them. Go does not accumulate heads: attestStore keeps the latest per (doc, signer) (attest.go:42-51), and offerAttest (:256-270) forwards each newer-seq attestation to the webview with no rate limit. So a Byzantine writer that sends rising-seq attestations with fresh heads grows #covered/#open without bound. This is not TR1 (Go trust) and not inventaire S3 (Go store keys). The « evicted heads still count » part has little security weight, since the signer is still a writer. Major, not critical: it needs sustained traffic from an admitted writer.

kept.title: Go and TypeScript CBOR profiles read a leading U+FEFF differently: TextDecoder strips the BOM
kept.question: go-equals-ts
kept.rule: §9.2.1 (spec.md:1674-1677): the receiver must refuse « exactement ce qui peut se lire de deux façons » (two decoders reading two different messages in the same bytes); §9.7 « Deux implémentations DOIVENT rendre le même verdict »
kept.evidence: frontend/packages/protocol/src/cbor.ts:22 `new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true })` (ignoreBOM defaults to false, so the BOM is removed) used at :70-75 for every text string, map keys included; protocol/repo/cbor.go:128-136 `utf8.Valid(raw)` then `string(raw)` keeps it. Checked: decoding EF BB BF 74 79 70 65 gives "type" (4 characters) in Node. No repo.json vector contains efbbbf.
kept.scenario: Bytes {"type":"sync", "﻿type":"request", ...}: TypeScript sees a duplicate key and refuses, Go accepts a sync. A documentId or senderId value prefixed with EF BB BF: TypeScript reads the bare id and accepts (admitted, authenticated), Go fails the regex or the equality and refuses. The same holds for every decoder built on decodeCBOR, including the live admission path (admission.ts:121).
kept.fix: Use `new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true, ignoreBOM: true })` in cbor.ts (and envelope.ts:133). State in §9.2.1 that U+FEFF is an ordinary character. Add vectors #utf8-bom-key (BOM key ignored as unknown, or a duplicate refused only when the texts are equal) and #utf8-bom-value (senderId with a BOM refused).

verdicts.reason: The divergence is real. cbor.ts:22 `new TextDecoder('utf-8', {fatal:true})` with the default ignoreBOM=false strips a leading U+FEFF, used at :70-75 for keys and values. protocol/repo/cbor.go:128-136 keeps the raw bytes after utf8.Valid. No repo.json vector covers it. Lowered to minor: on the live path only TypeScript judges repo messages, since protocol/repo is imported only by protocol/conformance/reference.go (grep). The TypeScript side is merely lenient, so the effect is a conformance/third-party disagreement and not an exploitable acceptance in inkwell.

Confirmed. cbor.ts:22 `new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true })` keeps the default ignoreBOM=false. Each non-stream decode() call at :72 therefore strips a leading U+FEFF, map keys included (:94-96, duplicate check on the decoded text). Go cbor.go:128-136 keeps the raw bytes. spec.md:1680-1682 defines duplicate keys by « textes décodés », so the two reference decoders give different verdicts on the same bytes. No vector has efbbbf. Lowered to minor: in inkwell only protocol/conformance/reference.go imports protocol/repo (Go never decodes repo messages live), and no harmful consequence was shown beyond a disagreement with a Go-based third party.

kept.title: Coverage tracks attestations for documents outside the admitted set; at the bound it refuses new ones first-come, so the per-signer share is not reserved
kept.question: spec-to-code
kept.rule: §4.10 (spec.md:486-487): the admitted set is the only list of documents « pour lesquels il garde des attestations »; §16.2 couverture (spec.md:2116): part réservée « par signataire », at the bound « les plus anciennes oubliées »; README rule 4 « Tout plafond partagé garantit une part à chaque pair ou à chaque personne qui écrit »
kept.evidence: WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:360-363 `#receiveAttested` passes any `doc` to `this.#coverage.attested` with no admitted check; coverage.ts:207-212 ignores a new document once the signer has 1024 or the total is 10 000 (`if (mine.size >= this.#maxDocsPerSigner) return; if (!this.#docs.has(doc) && this.#docs.size >= this.#maxDocs) return;`); coverage-bounds.test.ts:78-84 pins this first-come behaviour.
kept.scenario: Ten Byzantine writer devices each attest 1024 random, unadmitted document ids and fill the 10 000 global slots. An honest writer then attests a newly admitted document: coverage ignores it (:211), each change to that document is refused as uncovered (coverage.ts:302-310), and nothing reports it, so edits are lost silently.
kept.fix: Drop Attested envelopes for documents outside the admitted set, in the webview and in Go. Give each standing signer a reserved share ⌊10 000 / signers⌋ instead of a first-come total, and evict the signer's own oldest document at its bound as §16.2 says. Add a test where 10 hostile signers do not stop an honest signer's admitted document from being tracked.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:360-366 passes any doc to coverage.attested with no admitted check. coverage.ts:207-212 returns early (ignores the new attestation) once the signer has 1024 docs or the global map has 10 000. The spec row (spec.md:2116) says 'les plus anciennes oubliées'. 10 Byzantine writer devices can fill the global table, after which an honest writer's new document is never covered and its changes are refused silently.

Partly confirmed. WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:360-363 feeds any attested `doc` into coverage with no admitted-set check, against spec.md:486-487. coverage.ts:207-212 is first-come at 1024 per signer and 10 000 in total, with no per-signer reserved share. But one Byzantine writer cannot fill the 10 000 slots: only an admin can add devices (protocol/trust/list.go:288-305 IssueWith requires an admin), so it takes about 10 colluding writer devices. Lowered to minor. Not a duplicate of inventaire S3, which is the Go attestStore.

kept.title: The not-ready hold accepts a first message of up to 64 MiB per peer, against the 8 MiB bound
kept.question: spec-to-code
kept.rule: §9.4 (spec.md:1757-1758) and §16.2 « attente document non prêt » (spec.md:2112): 4 per document, 8 MiB per peer; beyond: refusal and rule H
kept.evidence: frontend/src/net/admission.ts:295-300 `(p.queue.length > 0 && p.bytes + bytes > 8 * 1024 * 1024) || bytes > 64 * 1024 * 1024`: an empty queue takes any message up to 64 MiB; protocol/limits.go DocumentPendingBytesPerPeer = 8 << 20 is used nowhere. The cooldown and reset on overflow (:301-306, WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:453-459) are inventaire R-Reset and are not re-reported.
kept.scenario: Each member device, readers included, sends one 60 MiB sync message for an admitted document that is not loaded yet. The webview holds 60 MiB per peer instead of 8 MiB, which is 3.8 GiB with 64 members, until the loader makes the document ready.
kept.fix: Refuse (with rule H) any message that would take the peer past 8 MiB, the first one included. A larger message for an unloaded document is a history-page case (§9.6), not a hold case. Add a bound test at 8 MiB and 8 MiB + 1 that reads the constant from protocol/limits.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. admission.ts:295-300: the 8 MiB test applies only when `p.queue.length > 0`, so the first held message is limited only by `bytes > 64 * 1024 * 1024`. spec.md:1757-1758 and the §16.2 row (2112) say 8 MiB per peer. Reachable by any announced member, readers included: Kind.Message needs only #member (WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:283), and hold is called before #enforce (:450-461) for an admitted, not-ready document (parsePeerMessage admitted check, admission.ts:153-158). Messages up to the legacy MaxFrame (~64 MiB, protocol/peer.go:29) can arrive. Distinct from BR1's Go output queue.

Confirmed. admission.ts:295-300 checks the 8 MiB bound only when `p.queue.length > 0`, so the first held message may be up to 64 MiB, against spec.md:1757-1758 / :2112 (8 MiB per peer). protocol/limits.go:236 DocumentPendingBytesPerPeer is unused. Messages above 8 MiB can arrive (mux reassembly 128 MiB). The retention is bounded (8x the per-peer bound, one per device, and only admins add devices), so minor rather than major. Not R-Reset, which is the overflow reset loop.

kept.title: The vector runners do not prove the refusal reason or check order: TypeScript ignores it, Go accepts two catch-all reasons
kept.question: proof
kept.rule: §12: a single order of checks, « une entrée qui échoue n'atteint jamais l'étape suivante »; README point 8 (vectors give expected outputs)
kept.evidence: frontend/packages/protocol/reference.ts:343-349: any throw counts as the expected rejection, and `expect.reason` is never read; protocol/repo/repo_test.go:131-135 `if got != reason && got != "invalid UTF-8" && got != "map key not a text string"` accepts either of those errors for any vector.
kept.scenario: A mutant that moves the admitted-set check before the senderId check, or that fails with a UTF-8 error instead of « duplicate map key », still passes #not-admitted, #wrong-sender and #duplicate-key in both runners.
kept.fix: Map each vector's reason to a stable error code exported by both packages (for example InvalidRepoMessage.code / repo.ErrCode), and make both runners compare codes exactly. Map the two Go aliases to their own vectors (#bad-utf8, #non-text-key) instead of accepting them everywhere.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. reference.ts:344-350 counts any throw as the expected rejection and never reads expect.reason. repo_test.go:131-135 accepts 'invalid UTF-8' or 'map key not a text string' in place of any expected reason. The reason and the check order are not proven by the vectors.

Confirmed. reference.ts:343-349 counts any throw as the expected rejection and never reads expect.reason. repo_test.go:131-135 accepts « invalid UTF-8 » and « map key not a text string » as the reason for every reject vector. Each repo vector has a single defect (repo.json listing), so no vector pins the order of checks in either runner. Go mutation is 99 % (gates/P3/SIMPLIFY.md), which softens this for Go but not for TypeScript.

kept.title: Several §9.2.1/§9.2.3 bounds have Go unit tests but no shared vector, so the TypeScript decoder is unproven on them
kept.question: proof
kept.rule: README point 8 (vectors a third party runs without inkwell); §16 preamble (spec.md:2056-2057) « un test par ligne vérifie la borne, la borne + 1 »
kept.evidence: repo.json holds 45 repo_message vectors (listed). None covers map of 65 pairs, array of 257, 4097 items, reserved additional info, a simple value (f8 xx), projectUrl of 81 characters, documentId of 65 characters or non-base58, sessionId/count, have of 257, changes of 257, or presence channel lengths. kept.fix: Turn each Go bound test into a repo.json vector at the bound and the bound + 1, so both runners use them. Add Stryker (capped through heavy.sh) for frontend/packages/protocol/src and frontend/src/net/coverage.ts, with the 95 % rule.

Confirmed. The 45 repo_message vectors (listed from protocol/vectors/repo.json) have no map-65, array-257, 4097-item, reserved-ai, simple-value, projectUrl-81 or have/changes-257 case. frontend/packages/protocol holds only cbor.test.ts (round-trips, :39-85) and conformance.test.ts. kept.title: protocol/repo uses its own literals instead of the exported §16 constants that TestLimitsMatchSpecification pins
kept.question: proof
kept.rule: §16 preamble (spec.md:2056-2057): « Les bornes sont des constantes exportées de protocol »
kept.evidence: protocol/repo/cbor.go:15-21 `maxDepth = 8 … maxSafe = 1<<53 - 1`; message.go:188 `1024`, :222 `1024`, :232 `80`, :123 `maxArray`; protocol/limits.go:205-228 CBORMaxDepth, MaxHandshakeBytes, MaxEphemeralBytes, MaxProjectURLBytes have 0 uses outside limits.go.

kept.fix: Make protocol/repo use the protocol constants (and @inkwell/protocol use a generated mirror checked against limits.json), so a single value drives the spec test and the codec.

kept.title: Points a third-party implementer must guess in §9.2: item counting, the nested ephemeral budget, check order for size
kept.question: proof
kept.rule: README point 10 (« la liste de ce qu'un implémenteur devrait deviner ... est vide »); §12 step 3 « taille ≤ borne du type » before step 6 « forme »
kept.evidence: spec.md:1690-1691 « plus de 4096 éléments au total » does not say whether map keys count; both implementations count them (cbor.go:83-86 for every item(), keys included at :174; cbor.ts:53 and :94). spec.md:1693-1694 applies the profile « au CBOR imbriqué du data des éphémères » without saying whether depth and items start again; both restart (message.go:191, repo.ts:244). The handshake 1024-byte and ephemeral 1024-byte checks come after the full decode in both (message.go:222, :188; repo.ts:175, :242), and the app checks the peer cooldown and ephemeral budget (WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:427-449) after the full parse (:422), against the §12 order 3 → 5 → 6.
kept.scenario: A third-party decoder that does not count keys, or that carries the outer item count into the nested data, accepts a 2100-pair-equivalent message that inkwell refuses: the verdicts differ on the same bytes.
kept.fix: State in §9.2.1 that each map key is one item, and that the nested data is a fresh value (depth 1, its own 4096). Move the size checks before decoding (and the budget before parsing in the adapter), or change §12 to the order implemented. Add vectors at 4096/4097 items counting keys.

verdicts.reason: Mostly holds. spec.md:1690-1694 does not say whether keys count as 'éléments' (RFC 8949 data items arguably includes them, which weakens that point) or whether depth and item counts restart in the nested ephemeral data. The order deviation is real: §12 (spec.md:1984-1989) puts size (3) and budgets (5) before the CBOR profile (6). The adapter instead calls parsePeerMessage (full decode, WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:421), then checks blocked (:426) and the ephemeral budget (:443). admission.ts:121 decodes before the handshake 1024-byte check (:133).

Weak but partly real. Counting map keys as items is the standard RFC 8949 data-item reading, so it is not a real guess. Whether the depth and item count restart for the nested ephemeral data (spec.md:1693-1694) is genuinely unstated, although both implementations restart (message.go:191 DecodeValue). The §12 order deviation is concrete: spec.md:1986-1989 puts size (3) and peer budget (5) before form (6), but WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:422 parses fully before the cooldown check at :427, and Go/TS check the 1024-byte handshake/ephemeral bounds after decoding (message.go:188, :222). No verdict difference was shown, only check order and cost.

kept.title: Undocumented webview behaviour on the wire path: ephemeral count must increase, re-arrive triggers re-attestation of every document, presence envelopes are kept with extra keys
kept.question: code-to-spec
kept.rule: §9.5 (spec.md:1762-1766) budgets only; §9.2.3 (spec.md:1710-1714) unknown keys « jamais conservées ni retransmises », closed envelopes refused (#presence-extra-key); §6.2 attestation flow
kept.evidence: admission.ts:259 drops an ephemeral whose `count` is not above the last one for the same sessionId, and :263 rewrites sessionId/count; neither is in §9.5. WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:493-498: every `arrive` from an announced peer calls `#reattest()`, which re-signs (attest.go:152-161) and gossips one attestation per document in #lastHeads, also undocumented. admission.ts:85-114 checks no key count on the `__presence` envelope (only the `MARKER` branch at :82 does) and returns the original `data` with unknown keys (:90, :94, :101) or re-encodes `...envelope, ...p` (:104-107), where the protocol refuses with « envelope is a closed map with one key » (repo.ts:247). This is one more rule gap behind AD1 finding 3, not a new decoder finding.
kept.scenario: A conformant third-party peer that restarts its count under the same sessionId has its presence dropped silently. A reader that re-arrives every 20 s makes each writer re-sign and broadcast up to 257 attestations per period. A presence envelope {__presence:…, x:…} reaches the Repo intact.
kept.fix: Either specify the count rule and the re-attestation trigger in §9.5/§6.2 (with a rate) or remove them. Re-attest only documents whose heads changed. Fold the envelope rule into AD1's switch to decodeRepoMessage.

verdicts.reason: Partly confirmed. In admission.ts:76-113 only the MARKER branch checks `Object.keys(envelope).length === 1` (:81-82). The __presence branch returns the original `data` (:90, :94, :101) or re-encodes `...envelope` (:104-107), so extra keys survive, against the closed-map rule (spec 9.2.3, vector presence-extra-key). The re-attestation on re-arrive (WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:492-496 → :389-391, with Go re-signing a new Seq at attest.go:152-161) and the count monotonicity (admission.ts:258) are also as described. Re-attestation is partly recorded as W58 residual R-5 (REVIEW.md round 5, row 1b).

(a) Confirmed: admission.ts:259 drops a non-increasing count for the same sessionId and :263 rewrites sessionId/count, and §9.5 (spec.md:1760-1766) does not say so. (b) Confirmed: #acceptHandshake (WailsNetworkAdapter.ts:487-498) calls #reattest on every arrive from an announced peer. #reattest (:388-390) re-sends every doc in #lastHeads with no sameHeads check, and Go sign() (attest.go:152-161) issues a new seq and gossips. The amplification is undocumented but bounded by the arrive rate (admission.ts arrive: burst 3, then 1 per 20 s). (c) Duplicate: the __presence extra-key gap (admission.ts:85-107) is a rule gap of the private decoder, AD1 finding 3, as the finding itself admits.
